teaser: A cost tool sees what agents spent; a behaviour policy says what each is for. Together they say whether the spend is right.
core_idea: A company that reads agent logs and token spend sees every token but not what each agent is for, so it cannot tell waste from the job. A behaviour policy with cost rows supplies that business context. In a worked example with an invented partner, Tallyline, and the invented Pellbridge Bank, each agent is judged against its mandate at published prices: about $9,320 a month falls to about $3,400. The support agent is waste, the AML reviewer is expensive and right, transaction reporting should use batch, and an agent with no mandate needs an owner. Mandates go one way, findings the other, and the logs stay with the customer.
